notes.title: Folk Emerging is a fascinating 4X strategy game about prehistoric nomads that ends where Civilization begins
notes.notes:
Folk Emerging describes itself as a turn-based 4X strategy game, but in practice, it's possibly more of a 2.5X strategy game, in that it puts you in charge of a nomadic hunter-gatherer community from before the rise of agriculture and the founding of towns and cities.

As this developer update suggests, it's like the turn or two at the very start of Civilization when you just have one Settler unit, but stretched out across thousands of years, with a social element and rustic spreadsheet aesthetics that remind me of King Of Dragon Pass. It's got somewhat doofy cartoon Stone Age muzak, but is otherwise the most intriguing Civlike strategy game I've laid eyes on since the one that looks like an octopus murder scene - and whadayaknow, by happy coincidence there's a public playtest running from right now till August 18th.

Read more

notes.title: Updated visuals & new features
notes.notes:
This is a quick update on some of the latest progress in the development of Folk Emerging.

[h2]Visual rework nearing completion🎨 [/h2]
The map art rework has gone well, and I've found an efficient workflow + style that I quite like. Here are some of the latest examples:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/80e1123063d70f0d706d22307213c098678225af.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/57c22bbe3e914eab89d33ce313629bfbe6493e54.jpg[/img]

[h2]Factions 🚩 [/h2]
I've added factions based on animal-worship, symbolizing the different values and tendencies of each tribe.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/a2502ab112b61e49360cbbc3345a128f261c69c0.jpg[/img]

[h2]Clan Relations  🤝 [/h2]
‪Each faction comes with 3 ancestral clans, and all individuals in your tribe belong to one of your 3 clans. The clans have evolving relationships with each other, from blood feuds to friendships. Each band is led by 1 of these clans, giving that band special advantages.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/aa63f0029bbf01fecafb493e6f8c38c2e235a5e9.png[/img]

[h2]Migratory Herds 🦣 [/h2]
Predators and prey are now also present directly on the map as migratory clusters, creating an even more dynamic environment for you to navigate.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/d1ff7c531cbe9a9798c647c715a90cb1a7a56acc.jpg[/img]

[h1]What's Next?[/h1]

Over the coming weeks and months I'll be working on the following gameplay features, whose design is mostly complete but remains to be implemented, in roughly this order:
[list]
[*] Tribe-level Climate XP
[*] Linking domestication to items & buildable structures
[*] Global climate change
[*] Local weather events
[/list]
After that on the horizon are features like:
[list]
[*] Loyalty & Cohesion
[*] Nested tooltips
[/list]
There are other features I'm excited about and designing at the moment, but which I'm not yet ready to share, as I want to first be sure they are a good fit for the game.

I'm on track with my ambition to get a good public demo ready for this summer's Steam festivals. I'll post more updates on this as it nears.

[b]Follow me on [url=https://bsky.app/profile/curiousdynamics.bsky.social]Bluesky [/url][/b] for more frequent updates (which is also a great place to check out the #TurnBasedThursday community and our weekly threads).

notes.title: Newest features and what's next
notes.notes:
This is a quick update on some of the latest progress in the development of Folk Emerging.

[h2]Visual rework continues 🎨 [/h2]
The map art rework is ongoing, and I'm excited about the painterly style that's slowly starting to come together. Here are some [b]work-in-progress[/b] examples:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/3dd742a659a2ce247d5bd0aca3686fc91492e8c1.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/ef113f5d597c2ef84dd8ab0a609307ed9e874819.jpg[/img]
There's lots left to improve, especially in terms of variation & randomization.

[h2]Territorial Claims 🚩 [/h2]
Tribes can now claim regions. A region in Folk Emerging is defined as any uninterrupted chunk of tiles that share the same climate and terrain (e.g. a chunk of 4 Steppe Hills tiles). Territorial claims here work a little differently to many 4X games, because everyone is nomadic, so you can choose to (or be forced to) leave a region you've claimed... and you can return.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/b5f1bb2fbd233839f1e3deeb3a3ac43aa33755d8.jpg[/img]
People's relationship to land was different in prehistory before sedentism and cities became dominant, and it's fun to research these themes and explore them in gameplay.

[h2]Buildable Structures ⚒ [/h2]
‪This is a feature I've been planning out for more than a year: as your prehistoric tribe develops it can eventually build structures like monuments, watchtowers, mines, farms ... and wonders like Stonehenge & more! 🗿

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/40c84cbc98e1c07ba066c371b7254a445b0cd8c0.jpg[/img]
Tribes can claim abandoned structures, fight over structures built by others, or destroy structures they want to remove from the map.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/e53a9dc31dab27abf97a68dd80fcc83bc840e5f1.jpg[/img]
Structures are built on the points between tiles, which creates interesting dynamics of conflict and collaboration, as each structure can be adjacent to up to 3 different tribes.

[h2]Chiefs & Councils 👑[/h2]
One of the forks in the road is whether you choose to have your tribe led by a Chief (a more authoritarian approach) or by a Council (a more egalitarian approach). Each comes with its own strengths, weaknesses, challenges, and opportunities.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/e4a85f409c2d1c5f209a6c26e19cea929d704864.png[/img]
In the first iteration of this system, the Chief's effectiveness is tied to their Reputation, while the Council's effectiveness depends on the relationships between the tribe's dynastic families. These factors are in turn affected by various other game systems, giving you many ways to solve the challenges that arise and adapt to your tribe's needs.

The Chiefdom approach is mostly implemented, and the Council system is coming soon.

[h2]Improved Text & Tooltips 📖[/h2]
I've added icons and better formatting to text and tooltips, which is especially helpful in tutorials.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/63d214e8979557feb70447cdd7e8f52c5a37302c.png[/img]

[h1]What's Next?[/h1]

Over the coming weeks and months I'll be working on the following gameplay features, whose design is mostly complete but remains to be implemented, in roughly this order:
[list]
[*] Inter-family relationships
[*] Council system
[*] Improved Band-splitting
[*] Loyalty & Cohesion
[*] Linking domestication to items & buildable structures
[/list]
After that on the horizon are features like:
[list]
[*] Factions
[*] Climate change & weather events
[*] Mobile herds
[*] Nested tooltips
[/list]
There are other features I'm excited about and designing at the moment, but which I'm not yet ready to share, as I want to first be sure they are a good fit for the game.

My ambition is to get a good public demo ready for this summer's Steam festivals. It's doable but requires keeping up the pace, nipping any scope-creep in the bud, and doing enough playtesting to squash sneaky bugs 🐞 I'll post more updates on this as it nears.

[b]Follow me on [url=https://bsky.app/profile/curiousdynamics.bsky.social]Bluesky [/url][/b] for more frequent updates (plus the turn-based gamedev & gamer community there is thriving).

Cheers :)

notes.title: Integrating autobattler combat system
notes.notes:
News updates on Folk Emerging slowed recently because I'm doing a visual overhaul with an artist and wanted to wait till that's done. But it'll take a while, and I'm too excited to share some new systems, so I'll be posting more updates with older [b]placeholder visuals[/b].

For example, I've been testing out the game with an [b]autobattler combat system[/b] instead of the old separate tactical grid system, and it seems to work quite well ⚔️  

It's been fun integrating the autobattler and 4X genres, as they're actually quite compatible. Here's a [b]gameplay snippet[/b] with the integrated autobattler prototype:

[previewyoutube=qyZz5cdQ-YA;full][/previewyoutube]

Auto-resolving battles between units on the main map is standard for 4X games, but there are [b]several ways to do it[/b], for example:
[list]
[*] In games like [i]Civilization [/i]and [i]Old World[/i], combat between two units resolves in a fraction of a second when the units collide, and the main focus being on which units you built and how you positioned them.
[*] Combat in games like [i]Europa Universalis[/i] or [i]Ara: History Untold[/i] auto-resolves over a few seconds/minutes, during which time you can send reinforcements, and the main focus is on your army's composition and the timing of your attacks. 
[/list] 

For Folk Emerging, I was interested in finding an alternative way to auto-resolve 4X combat that gives you [b] strategic agency[/b] in how you prepare your forces, but [b]resolves quickly[/b] and doesn't keep you away from the main map for long (which the old separate tactical map system did). I liked the side-view layout of games like [i]Darkest Dungeon[/i], which fits the prehistoric [b]"cave art" aesthetic[/b], and the mechanical simplicity of games like [i]Super Auto Pets[/i] where the battlefield situation is [b]clear at a glance[/b].

The autobattler game loop is some form of:
[list]
[*] fight battles
[*] get resources, upgrade & arrange your fighters
[*] fight more battles
[*] repeat
[/list]
The turn-based structure of the 4X genre is [b]perfect scaffolding[/b] for this. Each turn, you explore, gather resources, and build stuff. Some turns, you fight. The autobattler system is easy to integrate: before each fight, you can use what you've found/gathered/built to upgrade and arrange your forces to best [b]execute your strategy[/b].

There's so much in the tech tree, cultural norms, diet options, production choices, discoverable items, and event system that you can use to improve your autobattler units and make a [b]unique fighting force[/b].

There's a lot more to say on this front (e.g. how Individual tribe members factor into combat) and several other new systems, so keep an eye out for future posts!

[b]Follow me on [url=https://bsky.app/profile/curiousdynamics.bsky.social]Bluesky [/url][/b] for more frequent updates (plus the turn-based gamedev & gamer community is thriving there)

Cheers :)

Folk Emerging is indeed endlessly replayable and each playthrough is different because the map, characters, and stories are procedurally generated. notes.title: Publisher Talks & Visual Rework
notes.notes:
Hey there,

I've been working on finding a publisher for Folk Emerging, which is going well. It's important to find a publisher that truly understands strategy games and that will support its long-term development.

This process has also led to the decision to convert the map of Folk Emerging from 3D to 2D. This gives better results for less effort, time, and money. It makes it easier to achieve the desired aesthetic (90s history textbooks), it's easier to de-bug, and is more performant. 

So, I've got the game fully functional in 2D with placeholder visuals, and I'm excited to share some concept art and some work-in-progress screenshots of the rework!

[h1]2D map[/h1]

A [i][b]quick test piece[/b][/i] from a 2D artist:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/e93c235202cf63bc0b9022885623a57e40e85be2.jpg[/img]

Here are some [i][b]very early work-in-progress[/b][/i] screenshots using placeholder elements from the test piece:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/6fe6584cddde0c90c9839d2e83903bbe779c4606.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/559c272844c8fc87250fb059b33c3970abf2ac43.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/a02c835cbc21af9fee3fd837833585e90709f0e7.jpg[/img]

[h1]Gameplay Updates[/h1]

Here are some of the recent gameplay updates, addressing some feedback from the initial playtests and publisher talks:
[list]
[*] [b]Diet points[/b]: now multiple species can be food sources, with bonuses at each level as diet points accumulate for each species
[*] [b]Ecoregions[/b]: tile chunks with the same climate & terrain share a foodweb instance, and the entire ecoregion is highlighted when hovering over tiles
[*] [b]Less frequent Food choices[/b]: choosing a food source used to happen every turn, but now it only happens when entering new ecoregion or a food source has depleted
[*] [b]Impassable mountains[/b]: natural borders; all lowland chunks remain reachable
[/list]

Here is an example of how ecoregions are partitioned:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/7f2dc8f9605f48502ee487c20962f58e943af3bc.gif[/img]

There is a lot more in the works that is not yet ready to be shown. I'm holding off on a public demo for now, as publishers tend to want to be involved in demo releases, and I'd like to give the publishers I'm talking to a chance to participate. 

I look forward to sharing more updates soon!

Cheers :)

notes.title: First Private Beta Coming Soon 🎉
notes.notes:
Work on [i]Folk Emerging[/i] has steadily progressed over the summer, and it's almost time for the next milestone...

[h1]Playtesting[/h1]

Before releasing a public demo or sending builds to publishers, it's important to get the game into the hands of trusted players and get feedback. It's where the rubber meets the road, where the game makes contact with reality.

What works and what doesn't? What doesn't makes sense? Which parts are fun & interesting? These are all crucial questions that these private playtests will start to answer.

I would have liked to do this much sooner, but a 4X game juggles many systems, each of which needs to be fun and coherent on its own, [i]while also[/i] combining with all the other systems to create an overall experience that is fun and coherent too. 

It's tough to playtest a game like this until most of the components are relatively complete and inter-connected. Well, that time is nigh!

[h1]Recent Work[/h1]

Here are some updates on the work done in the last couple of months.

[h2]Victory conditions & playstyles 🏆[/h2]

I've been thinking a lot about what the win conditions should be. As Soren Johnson (designer of [i]Civ 4[/i], [i]Old World[/i]) points out in his excellent talk [url=https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1029133/Games-and-Meaning-or-You]"Games and Meaning, or You Have No Idea How Hard It Is To Run a Sweatshop"[/url], the entire player experience hinges on what they are told to aim for. 

Even if a game is intended to be "about" the unfortunate terrors of war, if a player is simply given an army and rewarded for conquering the world, then the game is actually "about" the thrill of conquest. They may still have a great time playing the game, but if the designers' goal was to have the player come away with a nuanced perspective on the matter, this is unlikely to happen. 

For me, Folk Emerging is about the [i]complex relationship between the individual and the collective[/i], and about [i]how humanity functioned before sedentism and centralized power[/i]. I don't want it to be about imperialist factions cosplaying as prehistoric tribes. 

So, I've been reading a lot of great perspectives on how to give strategy players a range of satisfying ways to play, e.g. rushdown / econ / defense, early / mid / late-game wins, tall vs wide, aggressive vs diplomatic, etc. 

For now, I've decided to set a simple goal of "be the first to reach X population", and give the player multiple routes to achieving that. It enables playing with different social structures, cultural norms, and technologies, which can result in a wide variety of human experiences & societies. 

I'm curious to see what the playtesters have to say!

[h2]Health ❤ [/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/dc9c167be45bf84bea040c9592702bb217387f4e.png[/img]

If the goal is to grow your population, then it's crucial that the health & mortality of your people work intuitively, and any changes need to be easy to track in the UI. Various events / states can affect HP, so I've tried to make all this easy to parse, both on an individual and collective level.

[h2]Plant & Animal Domestication 🌾🐖🐺[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/e95f1427c46a3d182e0c85b66dae9e377d0691b3.png[/img]

Humans have been domesticating other species for a very long time, with varied success. Domestication of plants began long before the agricultural revolution—it was just difficult, inefficient, inconsistent. Only after many thousands of years of struggle, innovations, and trial & error did we eventually enable a consistent food surplus, large populations, and sedentary settlements. 

I've added this process of gradual domestication to Folk Emerging. You can domesticate certain plants and animals from the start, but with little to show for it. The more experience your bands gain with each species, however, the better they'll get. Certain late-game technologies, combined with this hard-earned experience, enable massive increases in food yields from these domesticated species. 

With enough of a food surplus, maybe your nomadic hunter-gatherers can finally afford to stick around for a while... but is their society ready for it?

[h2]Social Norms ⚖️[/h2]

As a band's population grows larger, resources are spread thin and they have a choice to make:
[list]
[*] do they split up into 2 smaller bands and go their separate ways, to ensure everyone's survival?
[*] or do they stick together and weather the storm together?
[/list]
Each of these paths brings its own challenges, and requires different social norms to support it. 

If they choose to split up, how can they survive with dwindling ranks? Fewer mouths to feed also means fewer hands with which to defend your people. Can they maintain a connection to the family members and friends they've left behind? What is the cost of survival?

If instead they stick together and find a way to generate enough food for everyone, can their collective way of resolving inter-personal conflicts sustain a larger population, or will a more hierarchichal system be required? If an Individual is to be given the power to decide what's right or wrong, who should it be? What is lost in the process?

[h2]Production 🔨[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/90589e62da6fe26aa5fed3c63acd5e4661a48422.png[/img]

I've finally implemented a much-needed Production system. For a long time I avoided it, because each turn is 1 year of all the characters' lives, and I thought it would be weird to focus all of a band's efforts on 1 thing for multiple years. However, Civ gets away with cities "producing a Swordsman" for like 400 years so I guess anything goes!

Production is one of the main ways to give the player agency, and it can be framed as choosing what the band collectively puts their primary focus on, not that they aren't doing anything else during that time. For now, a band can "produce" the following (unlocked via the Tech tree):
 [list]
[*] specialized areas of their campsite, 
[*] improvements/upgrades to these specialized areas
[*] certain collective actions (e.g. scouting expedition, combat training, hunting exercises, etc)
[*] specialized combat units (each of which consists of 5 of your deeply simulated characters with personalities, skills, families, etc)
[/list]
[h2]Inter-Cell Features ⬢[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/196153c0370a6c1ad57f50075be736b3c669baa4.png[/img]

Rather than have 1 feature per tile, there are now up to 6 potential features per tile, as the features are placed at the 6 points of each hexagon. It also means that each of these feature borders 3 hexagons, so up to 3 different nomadic bands can gather around it. 

For example, 3 bands can gather around a Stone Deposit and have simultaneous access to Stone (an important resource in the game). Such a layout brings bands close together, enabling more interactions than just fighting over who gets to occupy a tile.

[h2]RPG-style Events & Special Items ✨[/h2]

Certain inter-cell features provide an opportunity to trigger an RPG-style event with various outcomes. For example, if you find a Cave and send a scouting party, they may find special Items, which you can choose to salvage and keep (for their various ongoing effects) or trade with other bands... hopefully the Cave doesn't collapse and fatally injure anyone from your scouting party 😱

[h2]Diplomacy 🤝 [/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/3f93514522838236673650f406a536849edc0fa5.png[/img]

I've implemented a basic trading system, via which bands can barter Resources (e.g. Food, Stone, Wood, Pelts) and Items (e.g. Obsidian, Amber, Shells). I'm planning to extend this system in various ways, and to enable some unique diplomatic options for those who pursue that playstyle.

[h2]Combat AI ⚔️[/h2]

For the playtests, the AI doesn't have to be amazing at combat, but they need to have some basic competence and unpredictability. Currently it's at a decent place with simple rules that work well enough for now.

[h2]Detailed Tooltips & Notifications 📃[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/da69ee49b633012565568c8470246b03530c318c.png[/img]

There's a lot going on under the hood, with many values affecting many others. I want it to be as transparent as possible without being overwhelming, so I've added on-hover tooltips wherever I can, with detailed breakdowns of how everything is calculated. I'd love to enable nested tooltips, but that's a nice-to-have for later.

I've also added notifications that inform you of important changes that happen throughout your turn and in the simulation between turns.

My goal is to enable players to easily understand the consequences of their actions and create their own fun & interesting strategies.

[h2]Stylized portraits & terrain 🎨[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/c01c40fdd7841b312f843ab2c6b1f914c198c09c.png[/img]

In early trailers/screenshots, the character portraits were 3D and colorful, but that didn't really fit the rest of the aesthetic. They are now stylized as charcoal drawings on slabs of stone, while retaining the complex (and heritable) facial features of the 3D models. Still need to make the eyes less creepy :)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/88dded13bfb2257ba2595688d5d596b25223ddfd.png[/img]

I also added a subtle paper texture to the terrain, which helps the vibe I'm going for: hand-painted illustrations from childhood history textbooks.

[h2]Save/Load System 💾[/h2]

Lots of us, myself included, love to take our time with these games and enjoy them over more than one sitting. It's a "simple" and expected feature but with complex simulations it can be a tough nut to crack — thankfully, 'tis now cracked.

[h2]Efficient content pipeline & potential moddability ♻️[/h2]

I've set up the game's content in a way that makes it very easy for me to tweak/add stuff, and leaves the door open for making the game moddable down the road.

[h2]Performance Optimization ✈[/h2]

I've implemented multi-threading to process the intense simulation that happens between turns (with great population comes great frame-droppability), which keeps the game running at a steady ~60 FPS, at least on my machine (the playtests will show how it fares elsewhere).

[h1]What's Next?[/h1]

Hopefully in a couple of weeks I'll be ready to start reaching out to gamer/gamedev friends (and others if they're super interested) to start playtesting! I'm very excited to get that started :)

This will help me sort out the biggest issues and have a build that can be sent to publishers. I'll gradually open up the playtests to a wider audience with the goal of polishing the game for a public demo.

notes.title: Got into the Earth Appreciation Festival!
notes.notes:
[i]Folk Emerging[/i] has been included in Steam’s [url=https://store.steampowered.com/sale/appreciateearth2023]Earth Appreciation Festival[/url]!

To celebrate the event, I’d like to highlight the game’s love for ecology, geography, and the wonders of our planet 🌍

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/9e7f65ff179236b93d5566c62fe2c7de5591313f.png[/img]

[i]Folk Emerging[/i] has several guiding principles based in biology:
[olist]
[*]Our physical environment has shaped our technologies and cultures.
[*]Resources are finite and have to come from somewhere.
[*]Collective behaviour emerges from individual actions.
[/olist]
In this post, I detail each of these principles.

[h1]Nature shapes Society[/h1]

[b]Our environment has been always instrumental in guiding humanity’s development. [/b]

It has influenced where we settle, which technologies we develop, and how our social norms evolve. This is why having realistic climates & maps is important to the game — the more detailed the climate simulation, the deeper it can explore the relationship between nature and society. I can recommend Lewis Dartnell’s book [url=https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/433955/origins-by-lewis-dartnell/9781784705435]Origins[/url] to those who want a deeper dive.

In fact, the whole project began as a hobby procedural map generator back in November 2021. I was nerding out over climate simulations and implemented my own version of the principles outlined in Artifexian’s [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5lCbxMZJ4zA]videos on realistic worldbuilding[/url]. It’s truly fascinating how our planet became the Earth we know, and I’ve loved learning about it.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/b11dae6859382125c73f5f33337e9d130865fa8b.gif[/img]
[i]^ Procedurally-generated earth-like map[/i]

A quick summary of how the procedural map generator works in the game: create elevation (e.g. mountains, flatland, oceans), simulate temperature & precipitation (e.g. based on winds, air pressure, oceanic currents), and combine all these ingredients to determine each tile’s final climate (1 of 12, based on a version of the [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification]Köppen climate classification[/url]). I plan to write another post going into more detail.

[h1]Resources: Finite & Costly[/h1]

[b]Resources are finite and have to come from somewhere.[/b]

In the game there are dynamic foodwebs from which food and other resources are extracted (at a cost). Humanity has a long history of disrupting ecosystems, but we also have a capacity for understanding and maintaining their balance. This is a core theme and mechanic in Folk Emerging.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/7bd59eb2b35fd4469fa5b82e2da04f9ec0464c79.gif[/img]
[i]^ Over-hunting a species (e.g. the Mammoth) can bring it to the brink of extinction[/i]

Each climate has a unique foodweb. As your group of hunter-gatherers migrates from region to region, you will choose their food sources, which will impact species’ populations. I’ve tried to capture the complexity of foodwebs by implementing a cascading effect: e.g. if you over-hunt the mammoths, the wolves have less to eat and their population dwindles too, so the rabbits are free to overpopulate, and they eat all the berries, and on and on… such cascades are a crucial part of our ecological reality and central to the game.

[h1]Emergent Collective Behaviour[/h1]

[b]Collective behaviour emerges from individual actions.[/b]

What do ant colonies, bird migrations, and human societies have in common? They’re all examples of nature’s emergent complexity. Folk Emerging explores that emergence in early hunter-gatherers by rooting every mechanic in individuals. Everyone and their grandmother is deeply simulated.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43707953/7d912825ac9602ef668cc65bee04d8408f252358.gif[/img]
[i]^ A social network visualization showing the familial relationships between tribe members[/i]

A tribe’s “technological progress” resides in the brains of its members; it’s a sum of their individual skills. Which resources are accessible, at what rates they can be gathered, and how much can be stored — all this depends on the abilities of the people in that group. In tactical combat, each unit represents deeply simulated characters. When one falls in combat, the tribe loses not only a fighter but also a skilled hunter, family member, and carrier of hard-won wisdom passed down through the ages.

[h1]What's Next?[/h1]

Be sure to check out the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/sale/appreciateearth2023]Earth Appreciation Festival[/url], and all the other games showing a world worth preserving. One of my favorites is [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1512050/World_Turtles/]World Turtles[/url], which comes out on May 1st!

https://store.steampowered.com/app/1512050/World_Turtles

In the meantime, I’m still hard at work on the demo for Folk Emerging, which is on track to be ready in a few months. At the moment I'm setting up key features, such as the save & load system, and making sure I can efficiently add new content. Can't wait to share the demo!

Cheers,
Curious Dynamics
